title: Jude
subtitle: a short, urgent letter from the brother of James
lead: Jude is one of the shortest books of the Bible: one chapter, 25 verses. Its writer calls himself "a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James," which most readers take to mean a brother of Jesus himself (Mark 6:3).

He meant to write about salvation, but he writes a warning instead: people have slipped into the church who turn grace into license. Jude answers with a rapid tour of Israel's history and Jewish tradition, quotes the Book of Enoch, and then turns to the faithful with commands to build, pray, keep and show mercy. It ends with one of the most loved blessings in the Bible: "Now to the one who is able to guard you from tripping..."
facts: Jude (Judas), "brother of James" (1:1), traditionally the brother of Jesus. Many critical scholars: a later writer using his name.
Uncertain. Traditional and many recent scholars: AD 50–70. Many critical scholars: AD 80–100.
Unknown. Probably churches of Jewish Christians, in Palestine, Syria or beyond, who knew 1 Enoch and Jewish tradition
A letter, mostly a warning sermon built on Scripture and prophecy, ending in a doxology
Greek, a rich, vivid style with many rare words

audience.to: Christians who were at home in Jewish Scripture and Jewish tradition. Jude names no city, but he expects his readers to know the wilderness story, the fallen angels of Genesis 6, Sodom, Cain, Balaam and Korah, and also 1 Enoch and a story about Moses that early writers say came from the Assumption of Moses, a book now partly lost. Many think that points to churches made up mostly of Jewish believers, perhaps in Palestine, Syria or the Jewish quarters of a city farther away. These churches shared meals together (the "love feasts" of 1:12), and teachers, perhaps traveling ones, had slipped in (1:4).
audience.why: To sound an alarm. Jude meant to write about "the salvation we share," but he writes instead to urge his readers "to fight hard for the faith that was handed down to the saints once for all" (1:3). The intruders turned grace into an excuse for sexual license, rejected the authority of Jesus as Master, slandered angels, claimed visions (if "dreamers" in 1:8 means that) and looked after themselves at the shared meals. Jude does not argue with their teaching point by point. He shows that Scripture and prophecy already describe such people and their end, and then he turns to the faithful: build yourselves up, pray, keep yourselves in God's love, and show mercy to those who waver. Knowing the readers explains his method. He quotes 1 Enoch and a story about Moses that his readers already knew and honored. Most scholars think Jude himself took Enoch's words as true prophecy. Either way, he argued from ground they shared.
views: Many scholars (Bauckham, Davids, Green) think Jude, the brother of Jesus, wrote in the 50s or 60s to Jewish-Christian churches, likely in Palestine or Syria, where his family was known and where 1 Enoch was widely read. The intruders were itinerant teachers who used Paul's message of freedom from the law as cover for moral license. Others think the readers may have been mixed or mostly Gentile churches: Gentile Christians read 1 Enoch too (the Letter of Barnabas, Tertullian), and turning Paul's message of grace into license suggests churches where Paul's teaching was known.
Later, a church facing early heresy

Other scholars think a later writer used Jude's name around AD 80–100. They often see the intruders as early forms of the teachers later called Gnostics, who claimed special spiritual knowledge and looked down on the body. Others answer that Jude says nothing about the ideas typical of later Gnosticism, only about behavior and authority.

Readers disagree on whether the intruders were outsiders passing through or members who had come to lead. Jude 1:4 says they "slipped in among you without being noticed," and 1:12 says they "shepherd themselves," which suggests teachers who took a leader's place and its support. Some link them to the error Paul answers in Romans 6:1 (sin so that grace may increase) or to the teachers of Revelation 2:14–15 and 2:20.

Most scholars think Jude treated 1 Enoch's words as true prophecy, since he says Enoch "prophesied" (1:14), though not necessarily as Scripture in the full sense. Others think he quotes a book his readers prized, and perhaps one the intruders used too, to turn it against them. The early church was divided: Tertullian accepted 1 Enoch partly because Jude quotes it, while Jerome reports that many rejected Jude for the same reason.

authorship: Jude, brother of James and of Jesus, wrote the letter himself. His brother James was famous enough to identify him; a forger would more likely have claimed to be an apostle or to be "the brother of the Lord." Its deep roots in Palestinian Jewish tradition fit a Galilean family. Defenders include Richard Bauckham, Peter Davids, Gene Green, Thomas Schreiner and Douglas Moo.

Many scholars think the letter was written in Jude's name after his death, as was common in Jewish and early Christian writing. They point to its polished Greek, its talk of "the faith that was handed down to the saints once for all" (1:3) and of the apostles' words as something remembered (1:17), which may suggest a later generation. J. N. D. Kelly and Jerome Neyrey give versions of this view, though many critical scholars also accept an early date.

Western tradition identified him with the apostle "Judas of James" (Luke 6:16), called Jude Thaddeus, the patron saint of lost causes in Catholic devotion. But "of James" there most naturally means "son of James," and Jude 17 speaks of the apostles as a group apart from the writer, so most scholars today distinguish the two.
outline: Greeting: to those called, loved and kept
Why Jude writes: fight for the faith, because intruders have slipped in
Three warnings: Israel in the wilderness, the angels, Sodom and Gomorrah
The dreamers slander what even Michael would not
Woe: Cain, Balaam and Korah; reefs, clouds, trees, waves and stars
Enoch's prophecy, and how it fits them
Keep yourselves in God's love and show mercy
Praise to the God who guards you from stumbling

lenses.name: Traditional
lenses.desc: A brother of Jesus writes an early letter (50s–60s) to real churches. Its examples and prophecies are true warnings. Held by most of the church through history and many evangelical and Catholic scholars today.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: A later Christian, writing in Jude's name near the end of the first century, defends settled doctrine against early heretics. Common in mainline scholarship of the 1900s.

lenses.name: Jewish-apocalyptic
lenses.desc: Jude reads Scripture and 1 Enoch like the Dead Sea Scrolls: old texts are prophecies of the last days, now fulfilled. Made influential by Richard Bauckham; it often supports an early date.

sections.b:
Jude is meant to be heard in one sitting. Read it aloud and listen for three things. First, the pattern: an example from the past, then "these people" in the present (see the chapter page). Second, the repeated words: "keep," "ungodly," "judgment," "mercy," "love." Third, the turn at verse 20: "But you, beloved." The letter is not only a denunciation. Its last word to the faithful is to keep themselves in God's love and to rescue others.

Jude assumes readers know the Old Testament well, and also Jewish traditions about angels, Enoch and Moses. The notes in the text supply that background.

sections.h: Jude among the books of the Bible
sections.b: Jude is one of the seven "general" or "catholic" letters (James, 1–2 Peter, 1–3 John, Jude), so called because most are addressed to the church at large. It was known by the late 100s, but Eusebius (about 325) counted it among the "disputed" books, and Jerome says many doubted it because it quotes 1 Enoch. Luther in 1522 placed it near the end of his New Testament with Hebrews, James and Revelation. Today every major church includes it. It sits just before Revelation, and its doxology makes a fitting doorway into that book.

No New Testament book is more at home in the Jewish world of the first century. Jude quotes 1 Enoch, retells a story from the Assumption of Moses, and uses traditions about Cain, Balaam and Korah that were later written down in the Targums (Aramaic paraphrases of Scripture read in synagogues) and the Mishnah (about AD 200). His method, reading old prophecies as fulfilled in "these people," resembles the commentaries of the Dead Sea Scrolls. Jewish readers have rarely commented on Jude, but scholars of ancient Judaism value it as evidence for how 1 Enoch was read.

Most of Jude 4–18 appears again, reworked, in 2 Peter 2:1–3:3. Most scholars think 2 Peter used Jude. Readers of both should compare them line by line: the differences show what each writer cared about. See the topic page .

reading: The landmark technical commentary. Shows Jude's Jewish method and argues for an early date by Jesus's brother.
Richard Bauckham, Jude and the Relatives of Jesus in the Early Church (1990)
On Jesus's family in the early church and Jude's use of Jewish tradition.
Peter H. Davids, The Letters of 2 Peter and Jude (Pillar, 2006)
Clear, readable and fair, with good background on 1 Enoch.
Gene L. Green, Jude and 2 Peter (Baker Exegetical Commentary, 2008)
A detailed Greek-based commentary, strong on the ancient setting.
Douglas J. Moo, 2 Peter and Jude (NIV Application Commentary, 1996)
A practical commentary that also explains the debates.
J. N. D. Kelly, A Commentary on the Epistles of Peter and of Jude (1969)
Jerome H. Neyrey, 2 Peter, Jude (Anchor Bible, 1993)
Reads Jude with tools from social science: honor, shame and group boundaries.
George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch: The Hermeneia Translation (2012)
A modern English translation of the book Jude quotes.

traditions.q: Is Jude as certain a part of the Bible as the books that were never doubted?
views: Yes. The Council of Trent (1546) listed all 27 books, Jude included, and declared that every one must be received as sacred and canonical in full. No book of the canon has a lower rank.
Yes. Jude was doubted by some early writers, but Athanasius listed it in AD 367 and the councils later received it. The church's acceptance over time is how the Orthodox know a book belongs.

Received, but Lutherans have kept a distinction. Luther placed Jude with Hebrews, James and Revelation at the back of his New Testament, and Martin Chemnitz said these once-disputed books should not be used alone to prove a doctrine; Lutherans today differ on how much this matters.

Yes. The Westminster Confession lists Jude among the books of the New Testament with no ranking. Their authority comes from God and is confirmed in believers by the inner witness of the Holy Spirit, not by how early they were accepted.
